title: Chapter 3 — Individualism Stronger At The Close Of A Democratic Revolution Than At Other Periods
paragraphs: The period right after the construction of a democratic society on the ruins of an aristocracy has just been completed is the one in which this separation of men from one another, and the selfishness that results from it, most forcibly strike the observer. Democratic communities not only contain a large number of independent citizens; they are also constantly filled with men who, having entered their independent condition only yesterday, are intoxicated with their new power. They have a presumptuous confidence in their own strength. Since they do not imagine they will ever need to call on the help of their fellow creatures again, they make no effort to hide the fact that they care for nobody but themselves.

An aristocracy seldom yields without a long struggle, in the course of which implacable animosities are kindled between the different classes of society. These passions survive the victory, and traces of them can be seen amid the democratic confusion that follows. Those members of the community who were at the top of the old gradations of rank cannot immediately forget their former greatness; they will long regard themselves as strangers in the midst of the newly formed society. They look upon all those whom this state of society has made their equals as oppressors whose fate can inspire no sympathy. They have lost sight of their former peers and no longer feel bound by any common interest to their fate. Each of them, standing apart, thinks he is reduced to caring for himself alone. Those, on the contrary, who were formerly at the foot of the social scale, and who have been raised to the common level by a sudden revolution, cannot enjoy their newly acquired independence without secret uneasiness. If they meet any of their former superiors on the same footing as themselves, they stand apart from them with an expression of triumph mixed with fear. It is, then, usually at the outset of democratic society that citizens are most inclined to live apart. Democracy does not lead men to draw closer to their fellow creatures; but democratic revolutions lead them to avoid each other, and perpetuate in a state of equality the animosities that the state of inequality produced. The great advantage of the Americans is that they have arrived at a state of democracy without having to endure a democratic revolution, and that they are born equal instead of becoming so.
